title: Data security, privacy and integrity, and the system around it

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: The difference between security, privacy and integrity of data; why both the data and the computer system need securing; and the security measures that protect a stand-alone computer system.

blocks.heading: Security, privacy and integrity
blocks.text: Three words, three different properties, and the whole topic rests on keeping them apart. Data security is protecting data from loss, corruption and unauthorised access: the file is there, unspoiled, and only the right people reach it. Data integrity is data being accurate, complete and consistent: the values are true and fit together. Data privacy is who is allowed to see particular data: personal data is limited to those with a right to see it. The properties can come apart, which is the test that keeps them apart. Data can be perfectly secure and still wrong: locked, encrypted, untouched by any outsider, with a mistyped dosage inside it, because a legitimate user made a mistake - so security does not give integrity, and integrity is protected by checking what is entered, not by stronger locks. Data can be accurate and open: a noticeboard of true figures that anyone reads, wrong for privacy though right on every value. Each property is protected by its own means - locks and access for security, checks and correction for integrity, rights and restraint for privacy - and an answer that protects one while naming another has missed the question. A question naming any of the three is first a question of which one: name the property the question asks about, name what that property is, and only then reach for the means, because the means follow the property and not the other way round.

blocks.heading: Why the system’s security is the data’s security
blocks.text: Data does not float: it lives on a machine, and the machine's health is the data's health. A failing disk corrupts the records stored on it; a power cut mid-save leaves a half-written file; protection software that is out of date welcomes the malware it no longer recognises; a network open to the internet carries strangers to the door. So data security needs the security of the computer system: the hardware kept working, the software kept current, the network filtered, the machine physically shut to strangers. A stand-alone computer is not safer by accident either: its risks come through the keyboard and the storage devices brought to it, so its measures answer those routes. The sentence to hold: the data is only as safe as the system that holds it, and every measure in this unit exists because somewhere that sentence was ignored. The stand-alone computer carries this duty too: no network connects it, so its risks arrive by keyboard and by brought-in storage device, and its measures - accounts, anti-virus scans of incoming files, updates kept current - answer those two roads, because a stand-alone machine is not an unthreatened one, only a differently threatened one.

blocks.heading: Measures that protect the system
blocks.text: The measures divide by what they check. User accounts with passwords restrict who may use the system at all, and each account's access rights decide what that user may reach - the till operator sees prices, not payrolls. Authentication techniques back the claim of identity: a password checks something the user knows; a biometric, such as a fingerprint or a face, checks something the user is, so the account opens to the person and not the knower of a word; and a digital signature checks who a message came from - the sender's software makes the signature from the message, and any receiver's software can check that the signature fits that message and names that sender, so a forged or altered message fails the check. Around the machine sit the guards: a firewall filters traffic between the computer or its network and the internet, blocking unsolicited connections from outside; anti-virus software scans files for known malware patterns and needs regular updates, because new malware appears constantly and yesterday's patterns miss today's; anti-spyware scans for and removes programs that record the user's activity and send it on. Encryption completes the set for data itself, and 6.1.2 gives it its proper home. Choosing among these measures is matching them to the routes onto the system: the keyboard is answered by accounts and biometrics, the arriving file by anti-virus and anti-spyware, the network by the firewall, the taken file by encryption - a measure aimed anywhere else guards a door the threat does not use.

blocks.heading: Common errors
blocks.text: The recurring slip is turning one property into another. Security and integrity explained the wrong way round: security protects from loss and unauthorised access, integrity is accuracy and consistency - the test is whether the data could be perfectly secure and still wrong, which it can, so they are different. And encryption given jobs it does not hold: encryption protects meaning once data is taken, not access or authorship, which 6.1.2's errors return to.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: The network whose threats 6.1.2 details is the network of 2.1, and the integrity that checking protects is 6.2's whole subject. The ethics of 7.1 begin here: data about people is where responsibility for people begins.
